Les Mamans du Congo : dénoncer à travers: Les Mamans du Congo: Speaking out through music
Rencontrez le groupe Les Mamans du Congo: Meet Les Mamans du Congo, a band whose songs encourage women’s emancipation.
(De gauche à droite) Robin, Zuangui, Pen: (Left to right) Robin, Zuangui, Penina, Mel and Gladys, of the band Les Mamans du Congo. Photo credit: Emmanuel Leroux-Nega.
Salut ! Depuis cet été, j’adore profiter: Hi! Since this summer, I’ve been loving all the festivities in Montréal! I was looking at the Festival International Nuits d’Afrique lineup and came across the band Les Mamans du Congo. I read their bio and thought: I have to meet them! I think it’s important to give media visibility to those who are making a difference, even on the other side of the ocean.
<strong>En 2018, Gladys Samba, ou <em>Ma: In 2018, Gladys Samba, or Mama Gladys, created a band to, as she puts it, defend women’s rights in Congo, Brazzaville. On stage, the artists use utensils, pestles, spoons, forks, baskets and salvaged objects, a nod to the chores associated with housewives. We met them the day before their show at the Festival International Nuits d’Afrique to ask them about the band’s goals.
Mardi 15 juillet, la journée est ensolei: Tuesday, July 15, a sunny day. We meet five members of the band: Gladys, founder and lead singer; Zuangui and Penina, the dancers; and two men, Mel and Robin, the percussionists and musical arrangers. Their hotel is just a few metres from Montréal’s Quartier des spectacles. Their luggage and instruments are still at the front desk; they’ve only just arrived from Quebec City, where their concert was cancelled because of thunderstorms.
Nous nous installons dans le jardin de l: We settle into the hotel garden. The artists sit on the chairs we’ve moved over, and the fatigue built up over the past few days is showing, on top of the heat. Gladys wears her love and pride for her roots on her wrist. It’s adorned with a bracelet bearing a gold-coloured pendant in the shape of the African continent. When they talk about the band’s founder, all the members call her “mama,” out of respect. “Congolese tradition teaches that when a woman turns 18, whether she has a child or not, she is already a mama, because she is a mother-to-be,” Gladys clarifies. “You have to say ‘ma’ in front of her first name. Once you’re over 40, you have to say ‘mama,’” Mama Gladys tells us. The same rule applies to men, with a “ta” placed before the first name.
Autour de son cou, Gladys porte un large: Around her neck, Gladys wears a large necklace of cowrie shells, and a navy blue and orange scarf is wrapped around her head. Music has been with her since childhood. “Inside, I was already preparing myself for music to be my passion and my job, even though my parents didn’t want it,” she says. “Growing up, in our cities and villages, there’s music everywhere. When you wake up, you hear the local papa playing his music to sell his beer! Music — we’re born with it, we die with it.”
Elle explique les motivations qui l’ont: She explains what drove her to create Les Mamans du Congo. “[Before], mamas couldn’t speak in front of everyone,” Gladys explains. Behind her, Mel nods. “Women had to stay home, in the kitchen, taking care of the children,” Gladys continues. “With the freedom of expression we have as artists, I said to myself, ‘Why not talk about that in songs, in shows, to get a message across?’” To her right, Robin listens attentively, arms crossed over his black sweater with multicoloured stripes.
L’émancipation des femmes, le travail co: Women’s emancipation and work as a driver of freedom are themes close to her heart. Even so, Mama Gladys doesn’t like the “feminist” label. What the band wants is to spread a message of equality for the women of her native country. “Women’s emancipation goes hand in hand with their tradition,” the singer maintains, index finger raised. “You have to know it in order to modernize it. You can’t go straight to modernization and leave the old days behind,” she says, brow furrowed. “Where is your foundation? To build a house, there has to be a foundation. And for us, our foundation is our tradition.”
Le groupe était de passage à Montréal, d: The band was passing through Montréal as part of its Canadian tour. Photo credit: Emmanuel Leroux-Nega.
Les instruments de cuisine choisis ne re: The kitchen tools weren’t chosen at random. “They’re our battle symbol,” Gladys says. Robin and Zuangui nod. “[A woman] can do other things besides laundry, dishes [...] and looking after her household.”
Gladys se réjouit que des femmes prennen: Gladys is glad to see women speaking out against the injustices they face. She gives the example of the collective<l1> Tosala, made up of 18 artists,</l1> founded in 2021, which raises awareness about women’s rights. Gladys is also determined to keep alive the heritage left by the elders, to make sure it doesn’t disappear, “to prepare the next generation,” she says. “[...] Every lullaby has its virtues back home. It’s not just to put children to sleep. Some of them help them grow, they give them phrases to hum, to start talking,” she says, pointing to her ear. “Back home,” she continues, “when a woman [gives birth], as soon as she gets home, there are traditional songs. People will come and sing for the child. So you hear music from the moment you’re born. People sing for you,” Gladys adds.
<strong>‍Fières de faire partie des <em>: ‍Proud to be part of Les Mamans du Congo
Zuangui rejoint la formation en 2022. El: Zuangui joined the group in 2022. She was 19 when Gladys took her under her wing. The band’s founder initially hesitated to include her, since she wasn’t a mother yet. “I went to see her parents to ask permission [for her to join the group] [...]. I saw her mom, her dad, her brothers, they asked me [what we do] in the group, and as soon as I talked about women’s struggle […], the first person who was interested was her father!” Zuangui tilts her head toward the ground and lets out a laugh. “Her father told me, ‘Take the child, I’m giving her to you! Because this is very important for our society.’”
« Avec ce qu’on vit dans notre pays, pou: “With what we’re living through in our country,” Zuangui continues, “I tell myself we have to defend this. It’s high time that we young people,” she says, pointing to herself, “take an interest in the situation [...].”
Quant à Penina, l’autre danseuse du grou: As for Penina, the group’s other dancer, she joined in 2020, at 26. “At first, my parents didn’t want me to, but I wanted to do it with love. In the end, I gave it my best. [In our] country, you can’t do two things at once. Back home, a woman’s place is in the kitchen, but I said to myself no, we have to stand up for ourselves,” Penina continues. Today, her family is proud of what she’s accomplishing, she says. They’ve often gone to see the band perform.
Les festivaliers ont appris des mouvemen: Festivalgoers learned dance moves at a workshop given by the band. Photo credit: Emmanuel Leroux-Nega.
Deux hommes sont présents aux côtés des: Two men sit alongside the three women: Mel and Robin. Mel, in a blue shirt with his locks tied back, is the band’s percussionist. Robin, seated at an angle, is a percussionist and musical arranger. Mel acknowledges the challenges Congolese women can face. “When I see the Mamans, I think of my mom,” Mel says. “I see the relationship my mother had with my father. […] We need balance,” he stresses, mimicking a scale with his hands. “[I’m] ashamed to see that men always want to be out in front. We’re different, each of us has something the other doesn’t.” Robin talks about his relationship with his two young sons: men can also play a role in the image of women they pass on to their children, he says. “We can’t bury our heads in the sand and say, ‘That’s not our job, it’s the mom’s,’” he stresses.
Après presque une heure de discussion, n: After almost an hour of conversation, we wrap up the interview and Mel showers Zuangui and Penina with compliments. “They seem shy, but on stage, you wouldn’t recognize them.” Everyone gets up, ready to go recharge their batteries before the big day.
